entities.name: Uluburun shipwreck
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Uluburun shipwreck, discovered off the coast of Turkey near the ancient city of Kaş, dates back to around 1304 BCE and serves as a critical archaeological site for understanding trade networks in the Late Bronze Age. This vessel, approximately 15 meters long, was laden with an extraordinary cargo, including over 20 tons of raw materials such as copper ingots, tin, and glass beads, which highlights the sophisticated maritime commerce that existed in the Eastern Mediterranean. The ship is believed to have traveled from the copper-rich regions of Cyprus or the Levant, indicating the interconnectedness of ancient civilizations and their reliance on trade for economic sustenance.

The shipwreck was uncovered in 1982 by marine archaeologist George Bass and his team, who meticulously excavated the site, yielding thousands of artifacts that illuminate the material culture of the time. Among these artifacts were Mycenaean pottery, Canaanite jewelry, and Egyptian scarabs, which offer insights into the cultural exchanges between the various polities of the ancient world. The ship's cargo demonstrates not only the economic transactions of the era but also the potential diplomatic ties and alliances formed through trade.

The legacy of the Uluburun shipwreck is profound, as it has reshaped our understanding of the Late Bronze Age and the complexities of ancient trade routes. The findings from the site have influenced subsequent archaeological methodologies and have inspired further research into maritime archaeology. Moreover, the artifacts have found their way into exhibitions worldwide, fostering an appreciation for ancient craftsmanship and the interconnectedness of early civilizations.
